title: Proud people. Fairer decisions. A listening loop that closes.
source: Your Voice master survey; analysis snapshot 30 October 2026.
notes: Open with the organisational question: what should Safewater Lines protect, and what should it fix first? People are proud and feel they belong. The gaps are in how people decisions are made and explained, and in whether leaders visibly act on what employees raise. We propose one 90-day pilot with three workstreams, measured with an anonymous pulse. Use the dashboard for questions rather than walking through every metric.

title:
Protect pride. Make people decisions fair
and visible. Close the listening loop.
source: item_evidence_profile.csv; priority_matrix.csv; priority_triangulation.csv; driver_model_summary.csv; group_hotspots.csv.
notes: Lead with the recommendation. Protect what works: pride, belonging and own-team support are all above 90% favourable. Priority 1 is fair, explainable people decisions, growth and recognition: the five lowest-scoring questions sit here, and Fairness is the block most strongly linked to recommending, satisfaction and intention to stay (31% of the explained variation). Priority 2 is leaders listening and visibly acting: it is the top actionable link to outcomes, the most common HR request and the most raised 'one change'. Cross-team handovers show a real but narrower gap; fix them in a targeted pilot starting in Customer Service. All links are associations from one survey, not proven causes.

title:
Pride and helpful colleagues
are assets to protect
source: item_evidence_profile.csv (PRI2, PRI1, CAM1); employee_voice_topic_summary.csv (preserve topic t); notebook §8.
notes: Three items show a strong foundation: 95.7% understand their contribution to business success, 92.4% are proud to work for Safewater Lines and 91.1% report help within their own team. In the 'what should we never lose' question, 119 respondents name their team or colleagues. Pride items are among the strongest associations with recommending and intending to stay (Spearman about 0.5–0.6), so protecting them matters for retention, not only for morale. Own-team support is high but only weakly related to the outcomes. Use all three as guardrails: the pilot should not erode them.

source: priority_triangulation.csv; priority_matrix.csv; hr_priority_counts.csv; one_change_topics.csv; grading rules fixed in notebook Step 7.3.

title:
One 90-day pilot, three workstreams,
clear accountability
source: implementation_roadmap_0_90_days.csv (adapted to the revised priorities); proposed actions, not approved commitments.
notes: Priority 1 is owned by the HR head with business heads: publish the criteria for appraisal, promotion and reward in the pilot roles, record and share the reason for each decision with a route to ask for review, and have managers give each person specific recognition every month. Priority 2 is owned by a leadership sponsor with HR: log every raised concern with an owner and a next-update date, publish a monthly 'you said, we did' update, and hold skip-level listening sessions starting in Customer Service. The handover pilot is owned by the Operations head with both team leads. All owners are proposals. No new platform is assumed. Specific accounts about facilities, respectful treatment or working-time boundaries need confidential verification through existing routes.

title:

source: implementation_roadmap_0_90_days.csv; roadmap_decision_gates.csv (adapted to the revised priorities); all standards and owners are proposals.
notes: Day 0 is organisational approval of scope, sponsor, owners and capacity. In the first 14 days, choose the pilot area (Customer Service first), review existing criteria and run an anonymous baseline pulse on the priority questions. Days 15–30 publish criteria, assign owners, open the concern-to-action log and agree the handover checklist. Days 31–60 run monthly recognition and updates, review handover exceptions weekly, and check burden and usefulness. Days 61–90 repeat the anonymous pulse, compare process measures, confirm pride and belonging held, and decide whether to scale, adapt or stop.

title: Methods were selected for the decision
source: ANALYSIS_FROM_DATA_TO_ACTION.md §12; notebooks/00_data_understanding_eda.ipynb, Step 7 and final methodology cell.
notes: Primary evidence is counts, distributions, favourable shares and paired comparisons. Working means assume equal category spacing and weights. Step 7 adds relative-weights analysis on 19 actionable questions (pride and belonging excluded as near-outcomes) with 500 bootstrap resamples, and a four-source evidence check with grading rules fixed before reading the result. Comment analysis uses 15 explicit overlapping topics with stance, assisted by AI and re-reviewed once; it is not independently validated. Exact bigrams and trigrams help navigate phrases. The topic network describes same-answer co-mentions and is prompt-sensitive. Sensitivity checks exclude straight-liners and use anonymous respondents only. None of these establishes causation.

title:
The priorities hold up under
the main robustness checks
source: item_evidence_profile.csv; priority_matrix.csv; named_vs_anonymous.csv; coding_review_before_after.csv; assistant_review_status.csv.
notes: Favourable shares fall when straight-liners are excluded and fall further among anonymous respondents, but the ordering of strengths and gaps is the same: pride stays high, and fairness, recognition and listening stay lowest. The driver ranking is identical without straight-liners (Spearman 1.00). Among the 100 anonymous respondents it shifts (Spearman 0.59): growth, fair rewards and leaders acting on feedback stay in the top tier, recognition rises into it and cross-team work drops out. That small group points the same way as the evidence check. The comment re-review covered 568 comments and changed 53 decisions; 75 cases still need context, and no independent coder was available.

title:
Use group patterns to guide listening,
not to assign blame
source: focused_group_profile.csv; cross_team_fairness_overlap.csv; whole-study n = 327; selected groups n ≥ 10.
notes: The 3–5-year tenure group and Customer Service are examples for further listening, not a ranking of problem groups. Eleven of 53 responses in the 3–5-year group show favourable own-team support and a 1–3 cross-team rating; 27 have at least one fairness item at 1–3. Corresponding Customer Service counts are 10 of 51 and 29 of 51. Departments and tenure groups overlap, so they are not independent comparisons. Composition, selection, role mix and working context could explain patterns. The heterogeneous Other grouping is unsuitable for a simple team-level diagnosis. Cross-team and fairness patterns overlap for 47 records but 90 records have a fairness item at 1–3 despite favourable cross-team collaboration, which is why the two themes should not be collapsed into one explanation.

title: The topic map helps organise discussion
source: topic_network_edges.csv; topic_network_parameter_sensitivity.csv; reports/network/topic_network_data.json.
notes: The full primary network includes 1,230 topic-coded suggestion/mixed answers from 305 response records, 13 displayed topics and 34 links supported by at least ten answers. This slide shows a selected five-topic excerpt using original node support and same-answer counts; positions are schematic, not analytical distances. Communication and teamwork co-occur in 98 answers from 93 records; 85 of those answers arise from the teamwork prompt. Fairness and career co-occur in 46 answers from 43 records; 41 come from the fairness prompt. Prompt dependence and parameter sensitivity limit any claim that the graph independently validates a mechanism. Node sizes represent unique-record support within the primary network context, line widths represent answer co-mentions. The offline interactive map provides question exclusion and further context.
